tips.title: il y a has two meanings
tips.body: Look at what **follows** it. A **noun** gives *there is*: *il y a un château*. A **length of time** gives *ago*: *il y a deux ans*. The test never fails, because *il y a deux ans* cannot mean *there are two years*.

tips.title: Is it still going on?
tips.body: If yes, it is **depuis** and the verb is in the **present**: *j'habite ici depuis deux ans*. If it is finished, **pendant** with a past tense. If it is a point, **il y a**.

tips.title: depuis flips the tense
tips.body: *J'habite ici depuis deux ans* is a **present** in French and a **perfect** in English — *I have lived here for two years*. Translating either half literally gives *I live here since two years*.

tips.title: Last admission is not closing time
tips.body: A leaflet prints both, and the question asks about the one you did not look at. *Dernière entrée à 17h45* with *ouvert jusqu'à 18h30* means arriving at 18h00 is too late.

tips.title: Do the arithmetic
tips.body: *Plein tarif 12 €, réduction de 25 %* has the answer **9 €**, and the number 12 printed on the page. The printed number is nearly always the distractor — as is the 12 in *moins de 12 ans*, which is an **age**.

why.matters: Visiting a town is reading: the leaflet from the tourist office, the opening times on the museum door, the prices at the desk, and afterwards the story of what you did. The topic exists because *il y a* has a second meaning, *ago*, that a reading text uses every year; because *depuis* and *pendant* both mean *for* and take different tenses; because the 24-hour clock and *fermé le lundi* are the small print that questions turn on; and because a printed price with a reduction has to be worked out, since the number on the page is usually the distractor.

examples.title: Il y a deux ans: ago
examples.body: *Il y a un château* is *there is a castle*; *il y a deux ans* is *two years ago*. What follows decides it: a noun gives *there is*, a length of time gives *ago*, and *ago* goes before the length where English puts it after. *Pendant* is *for* a length that is over, with a past tense; *depuis* is *for* a length still running, with the present. The test is one question: is it still going on?

visual.alt: A table separating il y a with a noun from il y a with a time, and pendant for a finished length from depuis for one still running

examples.title: Fermé le lundi
examples.body: The sign on the museum door is a set of traps. *Fermé le lundi* is closed every Monday; without *le*, just this one. *14h* is 2 pm and *18h* is 6 pm, the *h* standing where the colon would; *dernière entrée* is the last admission and not the closing time; *tarif réduit* is the reduced price and *gratuit* is free. Each is a reading question waiting to be asked, and the answers are in the small print, not the picture.

steps.title: En visite
steps.body:
Describing your own town and **visiting** one are different tasks. As a visitor you need what there is to see, how to find out, and what it costs.

**Where the information comes from:**

- **l'office de tourisme** — the tourist office
- **un plan de la ville** — a street map
- **un dépliant** — a leaflet
- **une visite guidée** — a guided tour

**What there is to see:**

- **le château** — the castle
- **la cathédrale** — the cathedral
- **le musée** — the museum
- **la vieille ville** — the old town
- **le marché** — the market
- **le port** — the harbour
- **les remparts** — the town walls

**Saying what you did there**, in the perfect tense:

- *J'ai visité le château.* — I visited the castle.
- *J'ai fait une visite guidée.* — I did a guided tour.
- *Je suis monté en haut de la tour.* — I went up the tower.
- *On s'est promenés dans la vieille ville.* — We walked round the old town.

**Visiter takes a place, not a person.** *Je visite Paris* is right; *je visite ma grand-mère* is not — for a person it is **rendre visite à**: *je rends visite à ma grand-mère*. English uses *visit* for both.

steps.title: Il y a, encore
steps.body:
You already know **il y a** as **there is** or **there are**: *il y a un château*. It has a **second meaning** that is completely unrelated, and it is one of the commonest reading traps at Higher tier.

$$\textbf{il y a} + \text{a length of time} = \textbf{ago}$$

- *Il y a un château.* — **There is** a castle.
- *J'ai visité le château **il y a deux ans**.* — I visited the castle **two years ago**.

**How to tell them apart**: look at what follows.

- **il y a + a noun** (*un château*, *des magasins*) → **there is / there are**
- **il y a + a length of time** (*deux ans*, *une semaine*, *longtemps*) → **ago**

That is the whole test, and it never fails. *Il y a deux ans* cannot mean *there are two years*.

**And the word order is the reverse of English.** French puts *il y a* **before** the length of time; English puts *ago* **after** it.

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *il y a deux ans* | two years **ago** |
| *il y a une semaine* | a week **ago** |
| *il y a longtemps* | a long time **ago** |

props.title: A noun after it means there is; a length of time after it means ago

visuals.alt: A table showing how to tell the two meanings of il y a apart by what follows it

steps.title: Il y a, pendant, depuis
steps.body:
Three expressions, all of them translated *for* or *ago* in English, and each doing a different job. Choosing between them is mechanical once you ask the right question.

**Ask: is it a point, or a length? And is it over?**

- **il y a** — a **point** in the past. *How long ago?* Takes a **past** tense.
  - *J'ai visité le musée **il y a deux ans**.* — two years **ago**.
- **pendant** — a length of time that is **over**. *For how long?* Takes a **past** tense.
  - *J'ai visité le musée **pendant deux heures**.* — **for** two hours.
- **depuis** — a length of time that is **still running**. *Since when?* Takes the **present**.
  - *J'habite ici **depuis deux ans**.* — I **have lived** here **for** two years.

**Depuis is the odd one out**, and in two ways at once:

1. It is the only one of the three that takes the **present** tense in French.
2. It is the only one English renders with a **perfect** — *I have lived*, not *I live*.

So *j'habite ici depuis deux ans* has a **present** in French and a **perfect** in English. Both halves of that have to be got right, in both directions.

**The test in one line:** if it is still going on, it is **depuis** and the verb is in the **present**.

steps.title: Lire les informations pratiques
steps.body:
Opening times and prices come up in **every** reading paper, and they are free marks if you can read the notation.

**The 24-hour clock is normal in French**, not formal. A leaflet will say *14h30*, never *2.30 de l'après-midi*.

- Subtract **12** from anything over 12: **14h** is **2 pm**, **18h** is **6 pm**, **20h** is **8 pm**.
- **12h** is **midday** and **0h** (or *minuit*) is **midnight**.
- The **h** replaces the colon: **9h**, **14h30**, **18h05**.

**Opening and closing:**

- **ouvert de 9h à 18h** — open from 9 am to 6 pm
- **fermé le lundi** — closed on Mondays. *Le* + a day means **every** Monday.
- **tous les jours sauf le mardi** — every day except Tuesday
- **dernière entrée à 17h30** — last admission at 5.30 pm

**Fermé le lundi** is worth a moment. Without *le*, *fermé lundi* would mean closed **this** Monday. **Le** makes it every Monday, and a question about whether you can go next Monday turns on that one word.

**Prices:**

- **plein tarif** — full price
- **tarif réduit** — reduced price, for students, children and the over-60s
- **l'entrée est gratuite** — admission is free
- **gratuit pour les moins de 12 ans** — free for under-12s

So a sign reading *plein tarif 12 €, réduction de 25 % pour les étudiants* means a student pays **9 €** — a saving of **3 €**. Reading questions ask for exactly that number, so do the arithmetic rather than copying the 12.

steps.title: Raconter une visite
steps.body:
Describing a visit you made needs the **perfect** for what happened and the **imperfect** for what things were like — and both of those you already have.

**What happened** — perfect:

- *J'ai visité la cathédrale.*
- *On a fait une visite guidée.*
- *Je suis monté en haut de la tour.*
- *On s'est promenés dans la vieille ville.*

**What it was like** — imperfect:

- *Il faisait beau.*
- *Il y avait beaucoup de monde.*
- *C'était magnifique.*

**Il y avait** is the imperfect of *il y a* — *there was* or *there were*. It is the form you want for describing a scene, and it never changes for number, exactly as *il y a* does not.

**And an opinion with a reason:**

- *Ce que j'ai préféré, c'était la vue depuis la tour, parce qu'on voyait toute la ville.*
- *Je le recommanderais, mais il vaut mieux y aller tôt.*

That last sentence does a lot for its length: a **conditional** (*recommanderais*), a **recommendation** and the pronoun **y**. Three structures in eleven words.

steps.title: À toi : une visite
steps.body:
**Partie A.** *Il y a* — *there is* ou *ago* ?

1. *Il y a une cathédrale au centre-ville.*
2. *J'ai visité Paris il y a trois ans.*
3. *Il y a longtemps, cette ville était un port.*
4. *Il y a un marché tous les samedis.*

**Partie B.** Complète avec *il y a*, *pendant* ou *depuis* :

5. J'ai visité le musée ___ deux heures.
6. J'habite dans cette ville ___ cinq ans.
7. Nous sommes allés à Lyon ___ un mois.

**Partie C.**

8. *Musée ouvert de 10h à 19h, fermé le mardi. Dernière entrée à 18h15. Plein tarif 8 €, gratuit pour les moins de 18 ans.* Tu as 15 ans et tu arrives à 18h30 un mercredi. Peux-tu entrer ? Combien payes-tu ?
9. Raconte une visite en cinq phrases : où, quand, ce que tu as fait, comment c'était, et si tu le recommanderais.

For question 6, ask yourself whether you still live there. If you do, only one of the three will work.

steps.title: Aller plus loin
steps.body:
**The two meanings of *il y a* are settled by what follows it.** A **noun** gives *there is*; a **length of time** gives *ago*. Nothing else is needed, and the test never fails, because *il y a deux ans* cannot mean *there are two years*. This is worth being certain about: it appears in reading papers every year, and a candidate who hesitates loses the sentence as well as the phrase.

**And the word order flips.** French puts *il y a* **before** the length; English puts *ago* **after** it. *Il y a deux ans* → *two years ago*. In translation, the phrase has to be turned round, not copied across.

**Depuis is doubly odd.** It takes the **present** in French and a **perfect** in English. *J'habite ici depuis deux ans* = *I **have lived** here for two years*. Translating either half literally produces a wrong sentence in the other language — *I live here since two years* is the classic. The test is simple: **is it still going on?** If yes, *depuis* and the present.

**Pendant is for a finished length; *il y a* for a point.** *J'ai visité le musée pendant deux heures* — I was there for two hours. *J'ai visité le musée il y a deux heures* — I went two hours ago. Same numbers, entirely different sentences, and reading questions use precisely this pair.

**Visiter takes a place.** For a person it is **rendre visite à**: *je rends visite à ma grand-mère*. English uses one verb for both, so this is a mistake you have to make deliberately not to make.

**Last admission is not closing time.** A leaflet gives both, and the question asks about the one you did not look at. *Dernière entrée à 17h45* with *ouvert jusqu'à 18h30* means arriving at 18h00 is too late — and 18h30 is printed more prominently.

**Do the arithmetic.** *Plein tarif 12 €, réduction de 25 %* has the answer **9 €** and the number **12** printed on the page. The printed number is nearly always a distractor. So is the *12* in *moins de 12 ans*, which is an **age**.

**Il y avait, not il y avaient.** The imperfect of *il y a* is invariable too: *il y avait beaucoup de monde*, whether one person or a thousand.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- **Visiter** takes a **place**; **rendre visite à** takes a **person**.
- **il y a + a noun** = **there is / there are**.
- **il y a + a length of time** = **ago** — and it goes **before** the length, where English puts *ago* after it.
- **pendant** = *for*, a length that is **over**, with a **past** tense.
- **depuis** = *for / since*, a length **still running**, with the **present** — and an English **perfect**.
- The test: **is it still going on?** If yes, *depuis* and the present.
- The **24-hour clock** is normal: subtract 12. **14h** is 2 pm, **18h** is 6 pm.
- The **h** replaces the colon: *9h*, *14h30*, *18h05*.
- **fermé le lundi** = closed **every** Monday. Without *le*, just this Monday.
- **dernière entrée** is **not** the closing time.
- **plein tarif** is full price, **tarif réduit** is reduced, **gratuit** is free.
- Work the price out: *12 €* less *25 %* is **9 €**. The printed number is usually a distractor.
- Recounting a visit: **perfect** for what you did, **imperfect** for what it was like.
- **il y avait** = *there was / there were*, and never changes for number.

questions.modelAnswer: **Une réponse complète :** *Je suis allé à Saint-Malo **il y a deux ans**. On **s'est promenés** sur les remparts et **j'ai fait** une visite guidée **pendant une heure et demie**. **Il faisait** beau et **il y avait** beaucoup de monde. Ce que j'ai préféré, **c'était la vue, parce qu'on voyait** toute la baie. **Je le recommanderais**, mais il vaut mieux **y** aller tôt.* **Ce qui compte ici :** - **Il y a deux ans** — *ago*, and before the length of time. - **Pendant une heure et demie** — a finished length, so *pendant*, not *il y a*. - **Je suis allé**, **on s'est promenés**, **j'ai fait** — the perfect carries what happened. - **Il faisait**, **il y avait**, **c'était**, **on voyait** — the imperfect carries the scene. - **Je le recommanderais** — the conditional, and **y** in *il vaut mieux y aller*. **Pour aller plus loin :** *hors saison, quand c'est moins touristique* adds a comparative and a qualification, which turns a recommendation into a judgement.

questions.prompt: Explique la différence entre *il y a*, *pendant* et *depuis*, et explique pourquoi *depuis* est le plus difficile des trois pour un anglophone.
questions.solution: Ces trois expressions se traduisent souvent par for ou ago en anglais, mais elles font trois choses différentes. Il y a indique un moment dans le passé et se traduit par ago : j'ai visité le musée il y a deux ans. Il faut noter qu'en français il y a se place avant la durée, tandis qu'en anglais ago se place après. Pendant indique une durée qui est terminée, et le verbe est au passé : j'ai visité le musée pendant deux heures. Depuis indique une durée qui continue encore, et c'est là que se trouve la difficulté. D'abord, depuis est la seule des trois à prendre le présent en français : on dit j'habite ici depuis deux ans, et non j'ai habité. Ensuite, l'anglais traduit cette phrase par un present perfect : I have lived here for two years. Donc les deux langues utilisent un temps différent pour la même idée, et l'erreur classique est de traduire mot à mot et d'écrire I live here since two years. Le test le plus simple est de se demander si l'action continue toujours : si oui, c'est depuis, avec le présent.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Les trois.**

- **il y a** — a **point** in the past: *ago*. *J'ai visité le musée il y a deux ans.* And it comes **before** the length, where English puts *ago* **after**.
- **pendant** — a **finished** length, with a **past** tense. *J'ai visité le musée pendant deux heures.*
- **depuis** — a length **still running**, with the **present**. *J'habite ici depuis deux ans.*

**Pourquoi *depuis* est le plus difficile.** It is odd in **two** ways at once:

1. It is the only one of the three taking the **present** in French.
2. English renders it with a **perfect**: *I **have lived** here for two years.*

So the two languages use **different tenses for the same idea**, and translating either half literally goes wrong. *I live here since two years* is the classic result.

**Le test.** Ask whether it is **still going on**. If it is, the answer is **depuis**, with the **present**.

examTechnique.body:
Decide which meaning il y a has by looking at what follows it: a noun, or a length of time.

Put il y a before the length of time, and remember English puts ago after it.

Ask whether the action is still going on. If it is, use depuis with the present tense.

Translate depuis with an English perfect, not a present.

Use pendant for a finished length and a past tense.

Use visiter for a place and rendre visite à for a person.

Read the last admission time as well as the closing time.

Work prices out rather than copying the number that is printed.

Recount a visit with the perfect for what happened and the imperfect for what it was like.
examinerErrors: Reading il y a deux ans as there are two years.
Writing deux ans il y a, copying the English word order.
Using the perfect with depuis instead of the present.
Translating depuis with an English present: I live here since two years.
Using pendant for a point in time, or il y a for a length.
Writing je visite ma grand-mère instead of je rends visite à ma grand-mère.
Answering a question with the closing time when the leaflet gives a last admission time.
Copying the full price when a reduction has been given.
Reading moins de 12 ans as a price rather than an age.
Writing il y avaient instead of il y avait.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer never hesitates over *il y a*, because it has a test rather than a memory: look at what follows. It chooses between *il y a*, *pendant* and *depuis* by asking whether the thing is a point, a finished length or still running — and it knows *depuis* changes tense in both directions, so it translates it as a perfect without being prompted. In a reading question it reads the whole notice, spots that last admission is not closing time, and does the arithmetic rather than copying a printed number. And recounting a visit, it separates the events from the scene, so the perfect and the imperfect each do their own work.
